verses.translation: And after{H310} this I saw{H7200} that an opening{H6607} was opened{H6605} — one{H259} — in the heavens{H8064}. And the first{H7223} voice{H6963} that I heard{H8085}, speaking{H1696} with me like the sound{H6963} of a shophar{H7782}, said{H559} to me: Come{H935} here, and I desire to show{H7200} you what shall be{H1961} after{H310} this.

one_way_hebrew: Uses שׁוֹפָר (shophar, H7782) — the ram's horn blown at Sinai (Ex 19:16,19, 20:18), on Yom Kippur (Lev 25:9), and at Jericho (Josh 6:4-20). Greek has σάλπιγγος (salpingos — 'trumpet'), a generic brass instrument. A back-translator from Greek would write חֲצוֹצְרָה (chatsotsrah, H2689 — the silver trumpet of Numbers 10:2) or transliterate. No translator encountering the generic Greek 'trumpet' would choose the specifically Israelite shophar — a ram's horn with Sinai covenant associations.

Uses שֶׁנִּפְתַּח פֶּתַח — the verb נִפְתַּח (niftach, niphal of פתח, 'was opened') immediately followed by the noun פֶּתַח (petach, 'opening/doorway'). This is a Hebrew wordplay on the root פ.ת.ח — 'an opening was opened.' Greek θύρα ἠνεῳγμένη ('a door having been opened') uses two unrelated roots (θύρα = door; ἀνοίγω = open), missing the Hebrew's internal sound play entirely. A back-translator from Greek would not reproduce this.

Uses רוֹצֶה לְהַרְאוֹת ('I desire to show you') — expressing personal will and desire (from רצה, H7521). Greek δείξω σοι is simply 'I will show you' — a neutral future. The Hebrew reveals the speaker's inner desire; the Greek merely states intention. A back-translator would write אַרְאֶה אוֹתְךָ ('I will show you'), not 'I desire to show you.'
greek_deviations: Hebrew: בֹּא לְכָאן ('come here'). Greek: Ἀνάβα ὧδε ('come UP here'). Greek specifies upward ascent (ἀναβαίνω); Hebrew uses the neutral בוא (come) without directional ascent.
Hebrew: 'I desire to show you' (personal will). Greek: 'I will show you' (simple future). Different modality.
Hebrew has a textual gap marked by brackets [ ] after רָאִיתִי, suggesting a lacuna in the manuscript. The Greek text has no corresponding gap.
translation_notes: 'Shophar' is transliterated rather than translated as 'trumpet' to preserve the specific instrument — a curved ram's horn, not a metal trumpet. The shophar's sound accompanied the giving of Torah at Sinai.
'Opening' for petach rather than 'door' — the Hebrew uses petach (an opening/entrance, H6607), not דֶּלֶת (delet — a physical door). The heavens have an opening, not a door with hinges.

הַמְדַבֶּרֶת (hamedabberet) uses the feminine participle form, agreeing with קוֹל (voice), which can take feminine agreement in Hebrew. This grammatical feature is native Hebrew and would not arise from translation.
textual_notes: The shophar at heaven's opening echoes Exodus 19:16,19 where the shophar sounds at Sinai as YHWH descends. The seer is summoned by the same instrument that accompanied the original theophany.
Brackets [ ] in the source text after רָאִיתִי indicate a gap in the manuscript — possibly a word or phrase lost in transmission.

verses.translation: And at once the Holy{H6944} Spirit{H7307} rested upon me, and I saw{H7200} one{H259} throne{H3678} set{H3427} in the heavens{H8064}, and upon the throne{H3678} one{H259} sitting{H3427}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses שׁוֹרֶה עָלַי רוּחַ הַקּוֹדֶשׁ ('the Holy Spirit rested upon me') — the Spirit descends UPON the prophet, the classic OT prophetic formula (cf. Num 11:25-26, Isa 11:2, 61:1). Greek ἐγενόμην ἐν πνεύματι ('I became in the spirit') reverses the direction — the prophet enters a spiritual state. These are opposite perspectives: Hebrew = the Spirit comes TO the person; Greek = the person enters THE spirit. A back-translator from Greek would write הָיִיתִי בָּרוּחַ ('I was in the spirit'), not 'the Spirit rested upon me.'

Uses תֵיכֶף וּמִיָּד — a doubled-emphasis phrase meaning 'immediately and at once,' a distinctly Hebraic intensification pattern (cf. Mishnaic Hebrew). The Greek has only εὐθέως ('immediately') — one word. No back-translator would spontaneously generate the Hebrew double-adverb construction from a single Greek word.

Uses יֹשֵׁב (yoshev, H3427) for BOTH the throne ('set/placed') AND the occupant ('sitting'). The same word describes the throne's establishment and the ruler's enthronement — a wordplay on the root י.שׁ.ב. Greek uses ἔκειτο ('was placed') for the throne and καθήμενος ('sitting') for the occupant — two different verbs. A back-translator would use two different Hebrew verbs too.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the Holy Spirit rested upon me' (Spirit acts on prophet). Greek: 'I became in the spirit' (prophet enters state). Opposite directional metaphor.

Hebrew: רוּחַ הַקּוֹדֶשׁ ('the Spirit of Holiness' — explicitly 'the Holy Spirit'). Greek: ἐν πνεύματι ('in spirit' — ambiguous, could mean 'in a spirit/ecstatic state'). The Hebrew is theologically explicit; the Greek is ambiguous.
translation_notes: תֵיכֶף (tekhef) is post-biblical Hebrew, common in Mishnaic literature. Its presence in this text reflects a Hebrew composition milieu, not a translation from Greek.

'Set' for the first יֹשֵׁב and 'sitting' for the second — both translate the same Hebrew word but capture the dual sense: the throne is 'seated' (established) in the heavens, and one is 'seated' (enthroned) upon it.
textual_notes: The phrase רוּחַ הַקּוֹדֶשׁ (ruach ha-qodesh — 'Spirit of Holiness') appears in Psalm 51:13 and Isaiah 63:10-11. It is also the standard rabbinic Hebrew term for the Holy Spirit, used throughout Mishnah and Talmud.

verses.translation: And the one sitting{H3427} upon it — his appearance{H4758} was like the appearance{H4758} of a sapphire{H5601} stone{H68} and jasper{H3471}. And around{H5439} the throne{H3678} was one{H259} bow{H7198}, like turquoise{H5306}.

one_way_hebrew: NEAR-VERBATIM from Ezekiel 1:26 — כְּמַרְאֵה אֶבֶן סַפִּיר ('like the appearance of a sapphire stone'). Ezekiel uses this exact phrase to describe the throne vision: כְּמַרְאֵה אֶבֶן סַפִּיר דְּמוּת כִּסֵּא (Ezek 1:26). The Hebrew Revelation preserves Ezekiel's distinctive vocabulary מַרְאֵה (mar'eh, H4758 — 'appearance/vision'). Greek ὅμοιος ὁράσει ('similar in appearance') is generic. A back-translator from Greek might use דוֹמֶה (domeh — 'resembling') or כְּעֵין (ke'ein — 'like the look of'), not the specific Ezekiel term.

Uses סַפִּיר וְיָשְׁפֵה ('sapphire and jasper'). Greek has ἰάσπιδι καὶ σαρδίῳ ('jasper and sardius/carnelian'). The Hebrew has DIFFERENT STONES in a DIFFERENT ORDER. Sapphire (סַפִּיר, H5601) appears in the Hebrew but NOT in the Greek; sardius (σάρδιον) appears in the Greek but NOT in the Hebrew. These are independent gem traditions — one cannot derive from the other.

Uses נֹפֶךְ (nofech, H5306) for the bow's color — one of the High Priest's breastplate stones (Ex 28:18, 39:11). Greek has σμαραγδίνῳ ('emerald'). A back-translator from Greek would transliterate σμαραγδ- or use בָּרֶקֶת (bareqet) or some other stone name, not the Torah breastplate vocabulary.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'sapphire and jasper' (סַפִּיר וְיָשְׁפֵה). Greek: 'jasper and sardius' (ἰάσπιδι καὶ σαρδίῳ). Different stones in different order.
Hebrew: bow 'like turquoise' (כמו נפך). Greek: bow 'like an emerald in appearance' (ὁμοία ὁράσει σμαραγδίνῳ). Different stone identifications.
translation_notes: 'Bow' for qeshet (H7198) — the same word means both 'rainbow' and 'war bow.' The Hebrew preserves this ambiguity; the word carries both the covenant sign (Gen 9:13-16, where God sets his qeshet in the clouds) and military imagery.
מַרְאֵיהוּ (mar'eihu) uses the archaic long possessive suffix -הוּ rather than the standard -וֹ. This is a feature of elevated/archaic Hebrew prose.
textual_notes: Ezekiel 1:26-28 provides the template: sapphire throne, a figure upon it, and a bow (qeshet) surrounding it. Ezekiel 1:28: כְּמַרְאֵה הַקֶּשֶׁת ('like the appearance of the bow'). The Hebrew Revelation reproduces this entire visual composition.

The breastplate stones (sapphire, jasper, nofech) connect the throne vision to the priestly garments — the divine throne is described in the same vocabulary as the High Priest's vestments (Exodus 28:17-20).

verses.translation: And around{H5439} the throne{H3678} were twenty{H6242}-four{H702} thrones{H3678}, and upon them sitting{H3427} twenty{H6242}-four{H702} elders{H2205}, clothed{H3847} in white{H3836} garments{H4403}, and upon their heads{H7218} crowns{H3804} of gold{H2091}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses כֶּתֶר (keter, H3804 — 'crown') — the royal crown of the Persian court (Esther 1:11, 2:17, 6:8). Greek has στεφάνους (stephanous — 'wreaths/victory garlands') — the athlete's or victor's wreath, not a royal crown. A back-translator from Greek would use עֲטָרָה (atarah — the standard Hebrew for stephanos) or would transliterate. No translator encountering the Greek victor's wreath would choose keter, the Persian royal diadem of Esther.

Uses לָבוּשׁ בְּמַלְבּוּשִׁים — 'clothed in garments,' an internal cognate construction where the verb (lavush, H3847 — 'clothed') and noun (malbushim, H4403 — 'garments') share the same root ל.ב.שׁ. This is a native Hebrew intensification pattern. Greek περιβεβλημένους ἐν ἱματίοις ('wrapped in garments') uses unrelated roots (περιβάλλω / ἱμάτιον). A back-translator would not spontaneously generate the Hebrew cognate pattern.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: כֶּתֶר (keter — royal crown). Greek: στεφάνους (stephanous — victor's wreath). Different types of headgear with different connotations.
Greek adds εἶδον ('I saw') — absent from the Hebrew.
translation_notes: 'Crowns' for keter — preserving the royal crown meaning rather than the victor's wreath implied by the Greek. These are not garlands of victory but royal diadems.

'Elders' for zekeinim (H2205) — the standard OT word for tribal elders, city elders, and the elders of Israel who stood before YHWH (Ex 24:9-11). The heavenly council of elders mirrors Israel's earthly governance structure.
textual_notes: The twenty-four elders may correspond to the twenty-four priestly divisions (mishmarot) established by David in 1 Chronicles 24:1-19 for Temple service. Each division served in rotation; all twenty-four are represented before the heavenly throne.
The white garments echo the priestly linen garments (בִּגְדֵי בָד — Lev 16:4) worn for service in the Holy Place.

verses.translation: And from the throne{H3678} went out{H3318} sounds{H6963} and thunders{H7482} and lightnings{H1300}. And seven{H7651} lamps{H5216} before{H6440} the throne{H3678}, and these are the seven{H7651} spirits{H7307} of YHWH{H3068}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses נֵרוֹת (nerot, H5216 — 'lamps') — the specific word for the lamps of the Menorah (Ex 25:37: וְעָשִׂיתָ אֶת נֵרֹתֶיהָ שִׁבְעָה — 'and you shall make its LAMPS seven'). The Hebrew sees seven MENORAH LAMPS before the throne — the heavenly Tabernacle's menorah. Greek has λαμπάδες πυρὸς καιόμεναι ('torches of fire burning'). A back-translator from Greek would write לַפִּידֵי אֵשׁ בּוֹעֲרִים ('burning torches of fire', cf. Gen 15:17), not the menorah-specific nerot. The Hebrew author identifies the seven lights as the menorah; the Greek translator rendered this as generic fiery torches.

Hebrew order: קוֹלוֹת וּרְעָמִים וּבְרָקִים ('sounds, thunders, lightnings'). Greek order: ἀστραπαὶ καὶ βρονταὶ καὶ φωναί ('lightnings, thunders, voices'). The orders are REVERSED. The Hebrew places 'sounds' first, matching the Sinai account where קֹלֹת (kolot — 'sounds/thunderclaps') comes first (Ex 19:16: קֹלֹת וּבְרָקִים — 'sounds and lightnings'). The Hebrew follows OT Sinai word-order; the Greek does not.

Uses שִׁבְעָה רוּחוֹת יַהְוֶה ('seven spirits of YHWH', H3068) — with the divine name. Greek has ἑπτὰ πνεύματα τοῦ θεοῦ ('seven spirits of God'). The Hebrew preserves the Tetragrammaton; the Greek substitutes the generic 'God.' A back-translator from Greek would write שבע רוחות אלהים ('seven spirits of God'), not YHWH.
greek_deviations: Hebrew order: sounds, thunders, lightnings. Greek order: lightnings, thunders, sounds. Completely reversed sequence.

Hebrew: נֵרוֹת ('lamps'). Greek: λαμπάδες πυρὸς καιόμεναι ('torches of fire burning'). Different objects — menorah lamps vs. burning torches. Greek adds 'of fire' and 'burning,' both absent from Hebrew.
Hebrew: 'spirits of YHWH.' Greek: 'spirits of God.' Different divine name.
translation_notes: 'Lamps' for nerot — preserving the menorah connection. These are the seven-branched lampstand's lamps, not generic torches.

'Sounds' for kolot rather than 'voices' — the word קוֹל means both 'voice' and 'sound/thunder.' In the context of thunder and lightning, 'sounds' captures the Sinai theophany meaning (Ex 19:16 uses kolot for thunderclaps).
textual_notes: Exodus 19:16 at Sinai: וַיְהִי קֹלֹת וּבְרָקִים וְעָנָן כָּבֵד עַל הָהָר וְקֹל שֹׁפָר חָזָק מְאֹד — 'And there were sounds and lightnings and a heavy cloud upon the mountain, and a very strong shophar sound.' The throne room vision recreates Sinai: sounds, lightning, and shophar (v1).

Zechariah 4:2-6 describes a golden menorah with seven lamps (שִׁבְעָה נֵרוֹתֶיהָ) and identifies them: 'Not by might nor by power, but by my Spirit, says YHWH of Hosts.' The seven lamps = the Spirit of YHWH is already an OT equation.

verses.translation: And before{H6440} the throne{H3678} was one{H259} sea{H3220} of glass, like the likeness{H1823} of crystal{H306}. And in the midst{H8432} of the throne{H3678} and around{H5439} the throne{H3678}, four{H702} living creatures{H2416}, full{H4392} of eyes{H5869} before them and behind them.

one_way_hebrew: Uses יָם (yam, H3220 — 'sea') — the word carries massive OT theological weight: the primordial chaos sea (Gen 1:10), the sea YHWH split (Ex 14-15), and the molten sea in Solomon's Temple (יָם מוּצָק, 1 Kings 7:23-26). The 'sea before the throne' directly parallels the bronze sea before the Temple. Greek θάλασσα ('sea') is neutral. While both say 'sea,' the Hebrew yam activates the entire Temple-cosmological complex.

Uses כִּדְמוּת (kidmut, H1823 — 'like the likeness of') — the EXACT word from Ezekiel's merkavah vision, used repeatedly (Ezek 1:5, 1:10, 1:13, 1:16, 1:22, 1:26, 1:28, 10:1). This is Ezekiel's signature visionary vocabulary. Greek ὁμοία ('resembling') is generic. A back-translator from Greek would write כְּמוֹ (kemo — 'like') or כְּעֵין (ke'ein — 'like the appearance of'), not the Ezekiel-specific demut.

Uses אַחְלָמָה (achlamah, H306) — one of the twelve High Priest's breastplate stones (Ex 28:19, 39:12). Greek has κρυστάλλῳ ('crystal'). A back-translator from Greek would write גָּבִישׁ or קֶרַח (ice/crystal), not the priestly breastplate gem. The Hebrew author consistently describes heavenly reality in breastplate vocabulary.

CRITICAL: Uses חַיּוֹת (chayyot, H2416 — 'living creatures') — the EXACT word from Ezekiel 1:5 for the four living creatures of the merkavah (chariot-throne): וּמִתּוֹכָהּ דְּמוּת אַרְבַּע חַיּוֹת ('and from its midst the likeness of four living creatures'). Greek ζῷα ('living beings') is a reasonable equivalent, but the Hebrew word directly invokes Ezekiel's specific vision. A back-translator might use בְּרִיּוֹת (briyot — 'creatures') or other terms, but the Ezekiel-trained Hebrew author naturally reaches for chayyot.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: צְלוֹחִית ('glass/flask' — a vessel word). Greek: ὑαλίνη ('glassy/of glass' — a material adjective). Same difference as in Rev 21:21.
Hebrew: כִּדְמוּת אַחְלָמָה ('like the likeness of crystal/amethyst'). Greek: ὁμοία κρυστάλλῳ ('resembling crystal'). Different comparison word and different material.
Brackets [ ] appear in the Hebrew text between וּבְתוֹךְ and הַכִּסֵּא, indicating a lacuna in the manuscript.
translation_notes: צְלוֹחִית (tselochit) is post-biblical Hebrew for a glass flask or vial. No standard Strong's number. It appears again in Rev 21:21.
'Living creatures' for chayyot — this is the standard translation of Ezekiel's chayyot. NOT 'beasts' or 'animals' — these are the angelic throne-bearers of the merkavah.
textual_notes: 1 Kings 7:23-26 — Solomon's Temple had a 'molten sea' (יָם מוּצָק) before the Temple entrance. The heavenly sea before the heavenly throne mirrors the earthly Temple's architecture. The Temple was built as a copy of the heavenly pattern (Ex 25:9,40).

Ezekiel 1:5,22 — the living creatures and something 'like the likeness of a firmament' (כְּעֵין הָרָקִיעַ) above them, 'like crystal' (כְּעֵין הַקֶּרַח). The sea of glass parallels Ezekiel's crystal firmament above the chayyot.

verses.translation: And the first{H7223} living creature{H2416} was like the likeness{H1823} of a lion{H738}, and the second{H8145} like an ox{H7794}, and the third{H7992} like a man{H120}, and the fourth{H7243} like an eagle{H5404}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses כִּדְמוּת (kidmut, H1823) for the lion — again the Ezekiel merkavah word — then switches to the simple כְּ (ke — 'like') prefix for the remaining three creatures. This MATCHES Ezekiel's pattern in Ezek 1:5,10 where דְּמוּת introduces the creatures and then specific faces are listed with shorter comparisons. A back-translator from Greek would use the same comparison word for all four (ὅμοιον appears for each in Greek).

Uses שׁוֹר (shor, H7794 — 'ox/bull') — a mature working animal. Greek has μόσχῳ (moscho — 'calf/young bull'). This MATCHES Ezekiel 1:10 which has פְּנֵי שׁוֹר ('face of an ox'), not a calf. The Hebrew preserves Ezekiel's specific animal; the Greek substitutes a younger animal. A back-translator from Greek μόσχος would use עֵגֶל (egel — 'calf'), not shor.

Uses כְּאָדָם (ke-adam — 'like a man', H120) — matching Ezekiel 1:5 where the living creatures have דְּמוּת אָדָם ('the likeness of a man'). Greek has ἔχον τὸ πρόσωπον ὡς ἄνθρωπος ('having a face like a man') — it adds 'face' (πρόσωπον) which the Hebrew omits. The Hebrew is closer to Ezekiel's phrasing.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: כְּשׁוֹר ('like an ox'). Greek: ὅμοιον μόσχῳ ('resembling a calf'). Different age of the animal — mature ox vs. young calf.
Hebrew: כְּאָדָם ('like a man'). Greek: ἔχον τὸ πρόσωπον ὡς ἄνθρωπος ('having a face like a man'). Greek adds 'face' — absent from Hebrew.
Hebrew: כְּנֶשֶׁר ('like an eagle'). Greek: ἀετῷ πετωμένῳ ('a flying eagle'). Greek adds 'flying' — absent from Hebrew.
Brackets [ ] appear in the Hebrew text before אַרְיֵה, indicating a gap in the manuscript — possibly a word like פני (face of) was lost.
translation_notes: 'Ox' for shor — NOT 'calf.' The Hebrew specifies a mature bovine, consistent with Ezekiel's vision.
'Man' for adam (H120) — the generic human/mankind term, connecting to the first adam of Genesis. Not אִישׁ (ish — 'a man/male individual') but the broader category of humanity.
textual_notes: Ezekiel 1:10 — וּדְמוּת פְּנֵיהֶם פְּנֵי אָדָם וּפְנֵי אַרְיֵה אֶל הַיָּמִין... וּפְנֵי שׁוֹר מֵהַשְּׂמֹאול... וּפְנֵי נֶשֶׁר ('the likeness of their faces: a face of a man, and a face of a lion on the right... a face of an ox on the left... and a face of an eagle'). The Hebrew Revelation preserves Ezekiel's EXACT animals: lion, ox, man, eagle — in the same creatures that Ezekiel saw.
The order lion-ox-man-eagle differs from Ezekiel's man-lion-ox-eagle but preserves the same four creatures. This reordering may reflect theological prioritization.

verses.translation: And to every{H3605} one{H259}, six{H8337} wings{H3671}, and within filled with eyes{H5869}. And they have no rest{H4496} day{H3117} and night{H3915}, and say{H559} continually{H8548}: Holy{H6918}, holy{H6918}, holy{H6918}, YHWH{H3068} of Hosts{H6635}, the Mighty{H117} — who was{H1961}, and is, and shall be{H1961}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL — VERBATIM QUOTE from Isaiah 6:3: קָדוֹשׁ קָדוֹשׁ קָדוֹשׁ יְהוָה צְבָאוֹת — 'Holy, holy, holy, YHWH of Hosts!' Isaiah's seraphim cry this before the throne. The Hebrew Revelation preserves the Isaiah quotation EXACTLY, including the compound divine name יהוה צבאות (YHWH Tsevaot). Greek has Ἅγιος ἅγιος ἅγιος Κύριος ὁ Θεὸς ὁ Παντοκράτωρ ('Holy holy holy Lord God Almighty'). A back-translator from Greek would write אֲדֹנָי הָאֱלֹהִים שַׁדַּי ('Lord God Almighty'), NOT the Isaiah quote. No translator encountering 'Lord God Almighty' would independently reconstruct the exact Isaiah 6:3 formula with YHWH Tsevaot.

CRITICAL — Uses הֶהָיָה וְהֹוֶה וְיִהְיֶה ('who was, and is, and shall be') — THREE FORMS of the root ה.ו.ה / ה.י.ה, from which the divine name YHWH derives. This is an ETYMOLOGICAL EXPANSION of the name YHWH itself: past (הָיָה), present (הֹוֶה), future (יִהְיֶה). The Hebrew author explicates what the name YHWH means — 'He who was, is, and shall be.' Greek changes the third element to ὁ ἐρχόμενος ('the coming one'), breaking the etymological connection to the divine name. A back-translator from Greek would write הַבָּא ('the coming one'), not יִהְיֶה ('shall be'). Only a Hebrew author thinking in Hebrew about the divine name would produce this tripartite formula.

Uses הָאַדִּיר (ha-addir, H117 — 'the Mighty/Majestic') — an OT divine epithet (Ps 8:2,10; 93:4; Ex 15:10-11; Isa 33:21). Greek has ὁ Παντοκράτωρ ('the All-Ruler/Almighty'). A back-translator from Greek Pantokrator would use שַׁדַּי (Shaddai — 'Almighty'), the traditional Hebrew equivalent. No translator would choose the distinctive OT epithet addir from the Greek compound word.

Uses מְנוּחָה (menuchah, H4496 — 'rest') — the theologically weighted 'rest' of the Promised Land (Deut 12:9: כִּי לֹא בָאתֶם עַד עַתָּה אֶל הַמְּנוּחָה — 'for you have not yet come to the rest'), of the Sabbath (Ex 23:12), and of God's own dwelling place (Ps 132:14: זֹאת מְנוּחָתִי — 'this is my rest'). Greek ἀνάπαυσιν ('respite/pause') is generic. A back-translator might use מרגוע or הפוגה, not the Land/Sabbath/Temple rest word.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: יַהְוֶה צְבָאוֹת הָאַדִּיר ('YHWH of Hosts, the Mighty'). Greek: Κύριος ὁ Θεὸς ὁ Παντοκράτωρ ('Lord God Almighty'). Entirely different divine title construction.
Hebrew: וְיִהְיֶה ('and shall be' — future of 'to be'). Greek: ὁ ἐρχόμενος ('the coming one'). Different concept — ongoing existence vs. coming/arrival.
Hebrew: 'within filled with eyes.' Greek: κυκλόθεν καὶ ἔσωθεν γέμουσιν ὀφθαλμῶν ('around and within full of eyes'). Greek adds 'around' (κυκλόθεν); Hebrew has only 'within.'
translation_notes: הֹוֶה (hoveh) — the present participle from the root ה.ו.ה. The consonants הוה are the core of the divine name יהוה. The author is spelling out what YHWH means through its verbal forms.

'Hosts' for Tsevaot (H6635) — meaning heavenly armies/organized forces. YHWH Tsevaot = 'YHWH of Armies,' the God who commands the angelic hosts. NOT 'Lord Almighty' — the Hebrew is specifically military/organizational.
textual_notes: Isaiah 6:1-3 provides the direct source: 'I saw the Lord sitting upon a throne, high and lifted up... Above it stood the seraphim: each one had six wings... And one cried unto another, and said: Holy, holy, holy, YHWH of Hosts.' The Hebrew Revelation reproduces: (1) the throne, (2) the creatures with six wings, (3) the exact trisagion formula.

The six wings connect to Isaiah's seraphim (Isa 6:2) rather than Ezekiel's chayyot which have four wings (Ezek 1:6). The Hebrew Revelation MERGES Ezekiel's four living creatures (chayyot with four faces) with Isaiah's seraphim (six-winged singers of the trisagion). This synthesis is native to Hebrew theological thinking.

verses.translation: And in the hour that the living creatures{H2416} give{H5414} praise and thanksgiving to the one who sits{H3427} upon the throne{H3678}, who lives{H2416} from everlasting{H5769} unto{H5704} everlasting{H5769} —

one_way_hebrew: Uses מֵעוֹלָם וְעַד עוֹלָם ('from everlasting unto everlasting') — the classic OT eternity formula appearing in Psalms 90:2 (מִן הָעוֹלָם עַד הָעוֹלָם אַתָּה אֵל — 'from everlasting to everlasting you are God'), 103:17, 106:48, and 1 Chronicles 16:36. Greek has εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων ('unto the ages of the ages'). A back-translator from Greek would write לְעוֹלְמֵי עוֹלָמִים ('for ages of ages'), not the Psalmic formula. The Hebrew preserves the Psalter's exact phrasing.

WORDPLAY: The חַיּוֹת (chayyot — 'living creatures') give praise to הַחַי (hachai — 'the Living One'). Both derive from the root ח.י.ה (to live). The LIVING creatures worship the LIVING God. Greek ζῷα... τῷ ζῶντι preserves some connection but the Hebrew wordplay is phonetically sharper (chayyot/chai).

Uses שֶׁבַח וְהוֹדָאָה ('praise and thanksgiving'). Greek has δόξαν καὶ τιμὴν καὶ εὐχαριστίαν ('glory and honor and thanksgiving'). Hebrew has two items; Greek has three. Hebrew lacks 'glory' and 'honor'; Greek adds them. A back-translator from Greek would include כבוד ויקר ('glory and honor'), not omit them.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: שֶׁבַח וְהוֹדָאָה ('praise and thanksgiving' — two items). Greek: δόξαν καὶ τιμὴν καὶ εὐχαριστίαν ('glory and honor and thanksgiving' — three items). Different lists.
Hebrew: מֵעוֹלָם וְעַד עוֹלָם ('from everlasting unto everlasting' — Psalmic formula). Greek: εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων ('unto the ages of ages' — Hellenistic formula).
translation_notes: שֶׁבַח (shevach) as a noun is more common in post-biblical and Aramaic usage (cf. Dan 2:23, 4:31). Its use here reflects the linguistic milieu of the Hebrew text.

הוֹדָאָה (hoda'ah — 'thanksgiving/confession') derives from the root ידה (yadah, H3034 — 'to give thanks/confess'). This root is used in Judah's name (Gen 29:35) and throughout the Psalms for thanksgiving.
textual_notes: Psalm 106:48 — בָּרוּךְ יְהוָה אֱלֹהֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל מִן הָעוֹלָם וְעַד הָעוֹלָם ('Blessed be YHWH, the God of Israel, from everlasting to everlasting'). This is the doxology closing Book IV of the Psalter, using the identical eternity formula.

verses.translation: The twenty{H6242}-four{H702} elders{H2205} were falling{H5307} before him{H6440} and praying{H6419} to the one who lives{H2416} from everlasting{H5769} unto{H5704} everlasting{H5769}, and casting{H2236} their crowns{H3804} before him{H6440}, and saying{H559}:

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses וּמִתְפַּלְּלִים (mitpalelim, hitpael of פלל, H6419 — 'praying'). This is the specific Hebrew verb for PRAYER — the hitpael reflexive form used throughout the OT for addressing God (1 Sam 1:10, 1 Kings 8:28, Dan 9:4). Greek has προσκυνήσουσιν ('they will worship/prostrate'). A back-translator from Greek proskuneo would use וַיִּשְׁתַּחֲווּ (vayishtachavu — 'and they bowed down/worshipped'), the standard Hebrew equivalent of proskuneo. No translator would render 'prostrate' as 'pray' (hitpalel). The Hebrew author sees the elders engaged in Jewish prayer, not merely physical prostration.

CRITICAL: Uses וְזוֹרְקִים (zorekim, H2236 — 'casting/dashing') — the specific PRIESTLY verb for dashing sacrificial blood against the altar (Lev 1:5,11; 3:2; 7:2; 8:19,24; 9:12; Num 18:17; 2 Kings 16:13; 2 Chron 29:22). The elders DASH their crowns before YHWH as a priest dashes blood. Greek βαλοῦσιν (balousin — 'they will throw/cast') is generic. A back-translator from Greek would use הִשְׁלִיכוּ (hishlichu — 'they threw') or הֵנִיחוּ (henichu — 'they laid down'), NOT the sacrificial zaraq. This verb transforms the scene into a priestly offering — the crowns become a sacrifice.

Uses לְפָנָיו ('before HIM') for where the crowns are cast. Greek has ἐνώπιον τοῦ θρόνου ('before the THRONE'). The Hebrew directs the offering to the PERSON; the Greek directs it to the FURNITURE. A back-translator from Greek would write לפני הכסא ('before the throne'), not לפניו ('before him').
greek_deviations: Hebrew: וּמִתְפַּלְּלִים ('and praying'). Greek: προσκυνήσουσιν ('and they will worship/prostrate'). Different actions — Jewish prayer vs. physical prostration.
Hebrew: 'casting (zaraq) their crowns before HIM.' Greek: 'casting (ballo) their crowns before the THRONE.' Different verb and different recipient.
Hebrew: כִּתְרֵיהֶם ('their crowns' — keter, royal diadems). Greek: στεφάνους ('their wreaths' — stephanos, victory garlands). Same distinction as verse 4.
translation_notes: 'Praying' for mitpalelim — preserving the specifically Jewish prayer-verb rather than generic 'worshipping.' The hitpael of פלל carries the reflexive sense of self-examination before God.

'Casting' for zorekim — though it may seem an unusual translation for what the elders do with their crowns, the priestly-sacrificial connotation of zaraq is essential. They do not merely 'throw' or 'lay down' their crowns; they OFFER them as a priest offers blood.
textual_notes: Leviticus 1:5 — וְזָרְקוּ בְּנֵי אַהֲרֹן הַכֹּהֲנִם אֶת הַדָּם עַל הַמִּזְבֵּחַ סָבִיב ('and the sons of Aaron the priests shall dash the blood against the altar around'). The same verb zaraq is used for the elders' crown-offering, making them priestly figures performing a sacrifice before YHWH.

verses.translation: Lord{H136}, you are worthy to receive{H3947} glory{H3519} and splendor{H8597}, for you are Creator{H1254} of all{H3605}, and by the hand{H3027} of your will{H7522} all{H3605} was made{H6213}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses בֹּרֵא (boré, H1254 — 'Creator') — the active participle of the verb used EXCLUSIVELY for divine creation in the OT (Gen 1:1: בְּרֵאשִׁית בָּרָא אֱלֹהִים — 'In the beginning Elohim created'). ברא is NEVER used of human making — only God בורא. Greek ἔκτισας ('you created') is a generic creation verb (κτίζω can be used of human founding of cities). A back-translator from Greek would use בָּרָאתָ (barata — past tense 'you created') as a verb, not the participial title-form בֹּרֵא ('you are Creator'). The Hebrew presents creation as God's ongoing identity — 'you ARE Creator' — not merely a past act.

CRITICAL: Uses עַל יַד רְצוֹנְךָ ('by the hand of your will', H3027 + H7522) — the Hebrew idiom עַל יַד (al yad — 'by the hand of/through the agency of') makes the divine will PHYSICAL and CONCRETE. The 'hand' (yad) of God's desire fashioned all things. Greek has only διὰ τὸ θέλημά σου ('through your will') — abstract, no hand. A back-translator from Greek would write בִּגְלַל רְצוֹנְךָ ('because of your will') or עַל פִּי רְצוֹנְךָ ('according to your will'), not the 'hand' idiom. The hand of God is a distinctive Hebrew theological motif (Ex 15:6, Deut 2:15, Josh 4:24, Isa 41:20, 48:13).

Uses אָדוֹן (Adon, H136 — 'Lord/Master'). Greek has ὁ Κύριος καὶ ὁ Θεὸς ἡμῶν ('the Lord and our God'). The Hebrew uses the single OT title Adon; the Greek expands to 'Lord AND our God.' A back-translator from Greek would write אֲדֹנָי וֵאלֹהֵינוּ ('our Lord and our God'), not the singular Adon.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: אָדוֹן ('Lord'). Greek: ὁ Κύριος καὶ ὁ Θεὸς ἡμῶν ('the Lord and our God'). Greek expands to a double title with possessive 'our.'

Hebrew: כָּבוֹד וְתִפְאֶרֶת ('glory and splendor' — two items). Greek: τὴν δόξαν καὶ τὴν τιμὴν καὶ τὴν δύναμιν ('glory and honor and power' — three items). Greek adds δύναμιν ('power'), absent from Hebrew. Hebrew has תפארת ('splendor'); Greek has τιμήν ('honor') — different concepts.
Hebrew: נַעֲשָׂה הַכֹּל ('all was made' — one verb, passive). Greek: εἰσὶν καὶ ἐκτίσθησαν ('they exist and were created' — two verbs). Greek adds 'they exist' (εἰσίν), absent from Hebrew.
translation_notes: רְאוּיָה (re'uyah — 'worthy') is a post-biblical Hebrew form from the root ראה (to see), meaning 'fit/fitting/worthy.' No standard Strong's number. Its feminine form here may agree with an implied subject or reflect late Hebrew gender flexibility.

'Splendor' for tiferet (H8597) — a word encompassing beauty, glory, and ornamental majesty. It is used of the priestly garments (Ex 28:2: לְכָבוֹד וּלְתִפְאָרֶת — 'for glory and for splendor') and of YHWH himself (Isa 60:19, 1 Chron 29:11).
'Creator' for boré (active participle) rather than 'you created' (past tense) — the Hebrew makes creation a defining title, not merely a historical event.
textual_notes: 1 Chronicles 29:11 (David's prayer) — לְךָ יְהוָה הַגְּדֻלָּה וְהַגְּבוּרָה וְהַתִּפְאֶרֶת ('Yours, O YHWH, is the greatness and the power and the splendor'). The same תִּפְאֶרֶת (tiferet) appears in this heavenly doxology as in David's earthly doxology.

Genesis 1:1 uses בָּרָא (bara) for divine creation. The participial form בֹּרֵא ('Creator') makes this a present-tense identity: the one on the throne IS and REMAINS the Creator. Isaiah 40:28 uses this form: בּוֹרֵא קְצוֹת הָאָרֶץ ('Creator of the ends of the earth').
Isaiah 48:13 — אַף יָדִי יָסְדָה אֶרֶץ ('indeed my HAND founded the earth'). The 'hand' of God as the agent of creation is a recurring Hebrew motif that the Greek text loses.

chapter_notes.summary: Revelation 4 in Hebrew is a throne-room vision built entirely from Ezekiel's merkavah (Ezek 1) and Isaiah's seraphim vision (Isa 6), expressed in native Hebrew theological vocabulary. The chapter contains at least 15 clear one-way translation markers — cases where the Hebrew could not plausibly derive from the Greek. The most powerful are: (1) The verbatim Isaiah 6:3 quotation (קָדוֹשׁ קָדוֹשׁ קָדוֹשׁ יַהְוֶה צְבָאוֹת) where Greek has 'Lord God Almighty'; (2) The tripartite YHWH-etymological formula הֶהָיָה וְהֹוֶה וְיִהְיֶה ('who was, is, and shall be') using three forms of the root from which the divine name derives, where Greek substitutes 'the coming one' for 'shall be'; (3) The priestly zaraq verb (v10) for the elders 'dashing' their crowns as a sacrificial offering; (4) The menorah-specific nerot ('lamps', v5) vs. Greek 'torches of fire'; (5) The shophar (v1) vs. Greek 'trumpet'; (6) Ezekiel's signature kidmut vocabulary (vv6-7); (7) The שׁוֹר/ox (v7) matching Ezekiel where Greek has 'calf'; and (8) The keter/royal crown (vv4,10) vs. Greek stephanos/victor's wreath. The chapter also uses breastplate gemstone vocabulary (sapphire, jasper, nofech, achlamah) to describe the heavenly throne, linking it to the priestly vestments. The Hebrew merges Ezekiel's four chayyot with Isaiah's six-winged seraphim into a unified throne vision — a theological synthesis that arises naturally in Hebrew but would not emerge from Greek back-translation.
